Ringstraked
RING-strakt
adjective
A compound of ring and straked (streaked), from Old English hring (ring, circle) + strica (a stroke, streak, line): marked with rings or encircling streaks. In the KJV it describes the ringed and streaked cattle of Jacob’s wages, rendering Hebrew 'āqod, striped or banded.

Biblical Definition

Ringstraked means marked with rings or encircling bands of colour—striped, banded, streaked round about—and it is the peculiar word for the mottled cattle that became Jacob’s hire in Laban’s house. When the wages were set, Jacob removed that day the he goats that were ringstraked and spotted (Gen 30:35), and afterward the flocks brought forth cattle ringstraked, speckled, and spotted (Gen 30:39). The colour of the beasts became the very ledger of the covenant, for Laban shifted the terms again and again: If he said thus, The ringstraked shall be thy hire; then bare all the cattle ringstraked (Gen 31:8). Whatever Laban named as Jacob’s wage, that the flocks bore, until it was plain that no cunning of Jacob’s and no fraud of Laban’s governed the increase, but the God of Bethel: I lifted up mine eyes, and saw in a dream, and, behold, the rams which leaped upon the cattle were ringstraked, speckled, and grisled (Gen 31:10). The ringstraked cattle are therefore a parable of providence writ in wool and hide. Laban meant to defraud; God meant to bless; and the striped and speckled flocks multiplied under the eye of the LORD who had promised Jacob at Bethel to keep him and bring him again. The believer’s wages are safe in such a hand: the God who could make the cattle bear whatever colour His covenant required can make all things serve the good of His own.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines RINGSTRAKED (ring-streaked) as having circular streaks or lines on the body; marked with bands or rings of differing colour.

expand to see more

RINGSTRAKED, a. — Having circular streaks or lines on the body; marked with rings or bands of differing colour. The he goats that were ringstraked and spotted (Gen 30:35).

RINGSTRAKED, a. — Streaked around, as a beast whose coat is banded with encircling stripes.

RINGSTRAKED, a. — Written also RINGSTREAKED; the older form retaining strake for streak.

STRAKE, n. — A streak, stripe, or line of colour; an old form of streak, surviving in this compound.

RING, n. — A circle, or that which encircles; here the encircling band of colour marking the beast.

Key Scripture

Gen 30:35 — "And he removed that day the he goats that were ringstraked and spotted, and all the she goats that were speckled and spotted, and every one that had some white in it, and all the brown among the sheep, and gave them into the hand of his sons."

Gen 30:39 — "And the flocks conceived before the rods, and brought forth cattle ringstraked, speckled, and spotted."

Gen 31:8 — "If he said thus, The speckled shall be thy wages; then all the cattle bare speckled: and if he said thus, The ringstraked shall be thy hire; then bare all the cattle ringstraked."

Gen 31:10 — "And it came to pass at the time that the cattle conceived, that I lifted up mine eyes, and saw in a dream, and, behold, the rams which leaped upon the cattle were ringstraked, speckled, and grisled."

Modern Corruption

Not a contested doctrine but a vivid old word for banded cattle; it recovers the providence of God over Jacob’s wages—the LORD making the very colour of the flocks serve His covenant against Laban’s fraud.

expand to see more

The word rebukes the fretful unbelief that thinks a man’s wages lie at the mercy of a defrauding master. Laban changed Jacob’s wages ten times, naming now the speckled and now the ringstraked as his hire, always seeking to leave him the barest portion. The age knows Laban well—the shifting bargain, the moved goalpost, the employer or circumstance that seems to hold a man’s living in its grip. But the ringstraked cattle answer the fret: whatever Laban named, the flocks bore, for the increase was not in Laban’s power nor in Jacob’s craft but in the hand of the God of Bethel. The striped and speckled beasts are a rebuke to anxious scheming and a comfort to honest labour under a hard master: the LORD can make the very wombs of the flock serve the wages He has appointed for His own.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereignty of God over a believer’s provision. Jacob had a promise from Bethel—I am with thee, and will keep thee—and that promise held through twenty years of Laban’s cheating, cashed out at last in ringstraked and speckled flocks. God did not spare Jacob the hard master, but He overruled the hard master to the keeping of His word. So the Christian need not fret over the Labans of his life; the God who could dictate the colour of the cattle can order every circumstance of his wages and his welfare to the good He has purposed, and none can defraud the man whom the LORD has undertaken to bless.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English hring (ring) + strica (streak) — marked with encircling bands; rendering Hebrew 'āqod (striped), the banded cattle of Jacob’s providentially guarded wages.

expand to see more

Old English hring — a ring, circle, or that which encircles; the first element of the compound.

Old English strica — a stroke, streak, or line; surviving as strake/streak in the second element.

Hebrew 'āqod (H6124) — striped, banded, ringstraked (Gen 30:35, 39; 31:8, 10, 12, of Jacob’s cattle).

Hebrew nāqod (H5348) — speckled, spotted (the companion term, Gen 30:32-33), naming the other markings of the flock.

English streak, strake — the surviving forms of the second element, keeping the sense of a line or band of colour.

Usage

"The ringstraked shall be thy hire; then bare all the cattle ringstraked—whatever Laban named as Jacob’s wage, the flocks bore, for God ruled the increase."

"The ringstraked cattle are a parable of providence writ in wool and hide: Laban meant to defraud, God meant to bless, and the striped flocks multiplied under the LORD’s eye."

"The believer need not fret over the Labans of his life; the God who dictated the colour of the cattle can order every circumstance of his wages to the good He has purposed."
